items.front: First command when you have a symptom and no idea which component is at fault?
items.back: kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -20 — the control plane narrates scheduling refusals, image pull failures, probe failures, volume errors and OOM kills into Events with a reason string.

items.front: Pod is Pending. What are the four causes?
items.back: Capacity (Insufficient cpu/memory), Taints (untolerated), Affinity/nodeSelector mismatch, PVC unbound. No events at all means the scheduler itself is down.

items.front: How do you read the logs of a container that is in CrashLoopBackOff?
items.back: kubectl logs <pod> --previous — the running container is a fresh restart with no history. Pair with 'describe pod | grep -A3 Last State' for the exit code.

items.front: Container exit code 137 with Reason: OOMKilled — what does it mean and what do you change?
items.back: SIGKILL from the kernel OOM killer: the container hit its memory limit. Raise it — kubectl set resources deploy/<d> --limits=memory=512Mi.

items.front: Pod is Running but 0/1 READY. Which probe, and what is the side effect?
items.back: The readiness probe. The Pod is not restarted, but it is removed from every Service's endpoints — so it presents as a networking failure.

items.front: Node is NotReady. What is the first thing to check on the node itself?
items.back: systemctl is-active kubelet, then journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager -n 50. The Conditions block of 'kubectl describe node' carries the kubelet's own message.

items.front: Node NotReady and every Pod stuck in ContainerCreating with 'network plugin is not ready' — cause?
items.back: The CNI is missing or broken. Check /etc/cni/net.d for a config and /opt/cni/bin for the plugin binaries, and whether the CNI DaemonSet Pods are running.

items.front: kubectl returns 'The connection to the server :6443 was refused'. Where do you work now?
items.back: On the control-plane node, with crictl and journalctl. Check /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml exists, then 'crictl ps -a --name kube-apiserver' and 'crictl logs <id>'.

items.front: How do you restart a control-plane component like kube-apiserver?
items.back: You don't. They are static Pods — edit the manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ and the kubelet recreates the Pod on file change. If it seems stuck, mv the file out, wait, mv it back.

items.front: Pods stay Pending with NO FailedScheduling events at all. Which component?
items.back: kube-scheduler. 'Created but never acted on' is the controller-manager's signature; 'acted on but never placed' is the scheduler's.

items.front: A Deployment is created but no ReplicaSet ever appears. Which component?
items.back: kube-controller-manager. Split it from a scheduler fault by asking whether the child object exists at all.

items.front: Service exists but ENDPOINTS is <none>. What are the three causes?
items.back: (1) Service selector doesn't match Pod labels, (2) Pods exist but are not Ready — unready Pods are excluded, (3) the Pods are in a different namespace.

items.front: Endpoints are present but connections are refused. What now?
items.back: targetPort doesn't match the port the app actually listens on, or the app is bound to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0.

items.front: How do you test DNS and connectivity from inside the cluster network?
items.back: kubectl run tmp --image=busybox:1.36 --rm -it --restart=Never -- sh -c 'nslookup svc.ns.svc.cluster.local; wget -qO- --timeout=2 svc.ns:80'

items.front: Difference between 'kubectl top node' and the 'Allocated resources' section of 'describe node'?
items.back: top shows live usage from metrics-server. describe shows requests already committed — which is the number the scheduler compares against. Different questions.

items.front: 'kubectl top' returns 'Metrics API not available'. What is the answer?
items.back: metrics-server is not installed. That IS the finding — not a command failure to work around.

items.front: How do you get logs from every container of a Pod, and from all Pods matching a label?
items.back: kubectl logs <pod> --all-containers, and kubectl logs -l app=web --all-containers --prefix --tail=50

items.front: A Pod is stuck Terminating. Why, and how do you force it?
items.back:
A finalizer is listed in metadata.finalizers, or the node is gone. kubectl delete pod

--force --grace-period=0 removes it from etcd without waiting for the kubelet.

items.front: Which two files on a node most often break the kubelet after an edit?
items.back: /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml (kubelet's own config: cgroup driver, staticPodPath, clusterDNS) and /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf (its kubeconfig to reach the API server).

items.front: Every node goes NotReady at once and the journal shows certificate errors. What do you run?
items.back: kubeadm certs check-expiration — expired control-plane/kubelet certificates take the whole cluster down in unison.

items.front: Before editing any static Pod manifest, what do you do?
items.back: cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/<file>.yaml /tmp/ — a typo'd flag crash-loops the component, and you may then be editing YAML with no kubectl and no undo.

items.front: Where does the kubelet look for static Pod manifests, and how do you confirm the path?
items.back: /etc/kubernetes/manifests by default. Confirm with: grep staticPodPath /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml

items.front: Imperative command for a Role granting read on Pods in namespace dev?
items.back: kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods -n dev

items.front: How do you bind a Role to a ServiceAccount, and what is the flag's exact form?
items.back: kubectl create rolebinding rb --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=<namespace>:<name> -n dev. For users it's --user=, for groups --group=.

items.front: How do you prove an RBAC grant actually works?
items.back: kubectl auth can-i list pods -n dev --as=system:serviceaccount:dev:app-sa — it asks the API server's own authorizer, the same code path a real request takes.

items.front: When do you use a ClusterRole with a RoleBinding?
items.back: When you want a reusable definition granted only inside one namespace. (Role + ClusterRoleBinding is invalid and does not exist.)

items.front: A Role grants 'pods'. Can the subject run kubectl logs?
items.back: No. pods/log is a separate resource — you need --resource=pods/log. Sub-resources are not implied by the parent.

items.front: Can RBAC deny a permission?
items.back: No — RBAC is purely additive. If a subject can still do something, look for a second binding (often to a group like system:authenticated), don't try to subtract.

items.front: Full etcd snapshot save command?
items.back: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key snapshot save /opt/snap.db

items.front: After 'etcdctl snapshot restore --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restore', what are the two edits in etcd.yaml?
items.back: (1) the --data-dir flag on the container command, and (2) the hostPath.path of the etcd-data volume. --data-dir is the container's view; the volume maps it to the host. Miss either and the restore serves stale data.

items.front: How do you verify a snapshot file without restoring it?
items.back: etcdctl --write-out=table snapshot status /opt/snap.db

items.front: You forgot etcd's certificate paths. Fastest recovery?
items.back: grep -E 'cert-file|key-file|trusted-ca-file|data-dir' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml — the manifest is this cluster's source of truth.

items.front: kubeadm upgrade: which command on the first control-plane node, which on every other node?
items.back: 'kubeadm upgrade apply vX.Y.Z' on the first control-plane node only. 'kubeadm upgrade node' on every other node, control plane or worker.

items.front: After 'kubeadm upgrade apply', what is still on the old version?
items.back: kubelet and kubectl — kubeadm never touches them. unhold, apt-get install the new versions, hold, then daemon-reload && systemctl restart kubelet.

items.front: Why does 'apt-get install kubeadm=1.35.0-1.1' silently install nothing?
items.back: The package is held (apt-mark hold) and/or the pkgs.k8s.io repo URL in /etc/apt/sources.list.d/kubernetes.list still points at the old minor version. Fix the URL, apt-get update, then unhold.

items.front: Can you upgrade a cluster from 1.33 straight to 1.35?
items.back: No — one minor version at a time: 1.33 → 1.34 → 1.35.

items.front: How do you get a working join command for a new node?
items.back: kubeadm token create --print-join-command — tokens expire (24h default), so the one from install time is usually dead. This mints a fresh token and computes the CA hash.

items.front: Correct order to remove a node from a cluster?
items.back: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force; kubectl delete node <node>; then on the node: kubeadm reset -f && rm -rf /etc/cni/net.d

items.front: Which kubeadm init flag must be set at install time for HA, and why can't it be added later?
items.back: --control-plane-endpoint <lb>:6443. It is baked into every generated kubeconfig and certificate SAN; adding it later means regenerating the PKI.

items.front: What does --upload-certs do, and what is its catch?
items.back: Stores CA material in a kubeadm-certs Secret so joining control-plane nodes can pull it. It expires after two hours; regenerate with 'kubeadm init phase upload-certs --upload-certs'.

items.front: How many failures does a 3-member etcd cluster tolerate? A 4-member one?
items.back: Both tolerate 1 — (n-1)/2. Even numbers add machines that can break without adding fault tolerance, so always use an odd count.

items.front: Stacked vs external etcd?
items.back: Stacked: etcd runs as a static Pod on each control-plane node (kubeadm default) — simpler, but losing a node loses an apiserver and an etcd member together. External: etcd on its own machines, failing independently.

items.front: How do you discover what a Helm chart lets you configure?
items.back: helm show values <repo>/<chart> — the defaults file names every key you can --set. Guessing key paths is the main way Helm tasks are lost.

items.front: Command to install a specific chart version into a new namespace?
items.back: helm install <rel> <repo>/<chart> -n <ns> --create-namespace --version 1.2.3. Without --version, Helm silently takes the newest chart.

items.front: How do you apply a kustomize overlay, and what is the common mistake?
items.back: kubectl apply -k ./overlays/prod. The mistake is 'apply -f kustomization.yaml', which tries to apply the kustomization file as an object. Preview first with 'kubectl kustomize ./overlays/prod'.

items.front: What are CNI, CSI and CRI, and where do you look for each?
items.back: CRI = how the kubelet runs containers (containerd; crictl; /etc/crictl.yaml). CNI = how Pods get network (/etc/cni/net.d, /opt/cni/bin). CSI = how volumes attach (kubectl get csidrivers, csinodes; the StorageClass provisioner).

items.front: Why crictl and not docker?
items.back: dockershim was removed in 1.24 — the kubelet talks CRI to containerd. crictl is the only way to see and log containers when the API server is down, which is exactly when you need it.

items.front: An operator was installed but nothing happens. What order do you check in?
items.back: (1) kubectl get crds | grep <group> — registered? (2) kubectl get pods -n <operator-ns> — controller running? (3) kubectl logs deploy/<operator> — what's it complaining about? (4) kubectl get <kind> -A.

items.front: How do you learn a custom resource's fields with no internet?
items.back: kubectl api-resources --api-group=<group> for the name/short name/scope, then kubectl explain <kind> --recursive for the whole schema.

items.front: What happens if you delete a CRD?
items.back: Every custom resource of that kind is deleted cluster-wide, immediately, with no confirmation.

items.front: Command to expose a Deployment on port 80 targeting container port 8080?
items.back: kubectl expose deploy web --port=80 --target-port=8080 — it copies the Deployment's own labels into the selector, which is the field most often typo'd by hand.

items.front: Valid NodePort range, and how do you pin one?
items.back: 30000–32767. kubectl create service nodeport web --tcp=80:8080 --node-port=30080

items.front: What does an empty podSelector ({}) mean in a NetworkPolicy?
items.back: It selects EVERY Pod in that namespace. Combined with policyTypes and no rules, that is the default-deny policy.

items.front: In a NetworkPolicy 'from' list, what is the difference between two dashes and one?
items.back: Two entries at the same level are OR (either peer). podSelector and namespaceSelector under a single dash are AND (a Pod matching both). One dash changes the meaning entirely.

items.front: Your NetworkPolicy applied cleanly and traffic still flows. Why?
items.back: NetworkPolicy is enforced by the CNI plugin. If the CNI doesn't implement it (plain Flannel, for example), the object is accepted and does nothing. Verify with a connection test, not with 'get netpol'.

items.front: Are NetworkPolicies additive or subtractive?
items.back: Additive — multiple policies selecting a Pod are UNIONed. There is no deny rule; a direction is denied only by having a policy in that policyType with no matching allow rule.

items.front: FQDN of a Service, and of a StatefulSet Pod?
items.back: <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local — and <pod>.<headless-service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local

items.front: How do you create a headless Service, and what does it return?
items.back: kubectl create service clusterip db --clusterip="None". DNS returns the Pod IPs instead of a virtual IP — how StatefulSet members get individually addressable names.

items.front: Where does CoreDNS keep its config, and how do you read its logs?
items.back: kubectl -n kube-system get cm coredns -o yaml (the Corefile); kubectl -n kube-system logs -l k8s-app=kube-dns

items.front: Imperative command for an Ingress routing app.example.com to service web:80?
items.back: kubectl create ingress web --rule="app.example.com/*=web:80" --class=nginx. A * suffix on the path means pathType: Prefix; without it, Exact.

items.front: Ingress has no ADDRESS. What's wrong?
items.back: No Ingress controller is running, or ingressClassName doesn't match one. An Ingress object is inert — a controller must be watching for it.

items.front: Ingress returns 503. Where is the fault?
items.back: The backend Service has no endpoints — so it is a selector/readiness problem, not an Ingress problem.

items.front: Name the three Gateway API resources and who owns each.
items.back: GatewayClass (infrastructure provider — which controller implements it), Gateway (cluster operator — listeners: ports, protocols, hostnames, TLS), HTTPRoute (application team — matches and backendRefs, attached via parentRefs).

items.front: How do you tell whether an HTTPRoute actually attached to its Gateway?
items.back: kubectl describe httproute <name> — status.parents[].conditions. Common reasons for failure: NotAllowedByListeners (the Gateway's allowedRoutes.namespaces excludes yours) or NoMatchingParent.

items.front: 'kubectl get gateway' says the server doesn't have that resource type. What's wrong?
items.back: The Gateway API CRDs are not installed — they don't ship with Kubernetes. Nothing is wrong with your YAML.

items.front: Update a Deployment's image without an editor?
items.back: kubectl set image deploy/web nginx=nginx:1.27 — the form is container-name=new-image. It patches one field and triggers exactly one rollout.

items.front: You changed a mounted ConfigMap. How do you make the Pods pick it up?
items.back: kubectl rollout restart deploy/<d> — it stamps a new annotation on the Pod template, which is a template change, which rolls the Deployment.

items.front: Roll back to a specific revision?
items.back: kubectl rollout undo deploy/web --to-revision=2 (list them with kubectl rollout history deploy/web)

items.front: Which rollingUpdate settings give zero downtime, and why?
items.back: maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 — a new Pod must become Ready before an old one is removed.

items.front: Difference between --from-file and --from-env-file when creating a ConfigMap?
items.back: --from-file gives ONE key (the filename) whose value is the whole file. --from-env-file gives one key per KEY=value line.

items.front: Inject every key of a ConfigMap as environment variables?
items.back: kubectl set env deploy/web --from=configmap/app-cfg (a trailing dash on a name, e.g. LOG_LEVEL-, removes a variable)

items.front: Read a Secret's value back as plaintext?
items.back: kubectl get secret db-cred -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d — Secret values are base64 in the API, not encrypted.

items.front: HPA shows TARGETS as <unknown>/70%. Two causes?
items.back: metrics-server isn't installed (kubectl top also fails), or the Deployment declares no CPU *request* — the percentage is of the request, so with no request there is no denominator.

items.front: Create an HPA imperatively?
items.back: kubectl autoscale deploy web --min=2 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70

items.front: Trigger a CronJob immediately, out of schedule?
items.back: kubectl create job manual-run --from=cronjob/report

items.front: kubectl drain hangs on 'cannot evict pod as it would violate the disruption budget'. What is it?
items.back: A PodDisruptionBudget — working as designed. It sets a floor on availability during voluntary disruption. Scale up, or relax/remove the PDB.

items.front: Which taint effect evicts Pods that are already running?
items.back: NoExecute. NoSchedule and PreferNoSchedule only affect future scheduling, so they look like they did nothing.

items.front: Remove a taint from a node?
items.back: kubectl taint nodes worker-1 gpu=true:NoSchedule-  — the trailing dash means remove.

items.front: After you add a ResourceQuota for cpu/memory, new Pods are rejected. Why, and what fixes it?
items.back: Once a quota constrains cpu or memory, every Pod in that namespace must declare matching requests/limits or admission rejects it. A LimitRange supplies defaults.

items.front: How do you delete a static Pod?
items.back: Move its manifest out of /etc/kubernetes/manifests. kubectl delete just makes the kubelet recreate it.

items.front: Three conditions for a PV to bind to a PVC?
items.back: capacity >= request, accessModes a superset of the claim's, and storageClassName matching exactly — including the empty string.

items.front: storageClassName: "" vs omitting the field?
items.back: "" means 'explicitly no class — static binding only'. Omitting it means 'use the default StorageClass'. With no default class, omitting it leaves the PVC Pending forever.

items.front: PVC event says 'waiting for first consumer to be created before binding'. Is this a fault?
items.back: No — the StorageClass uses volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer. Binding happens when a Pod that uses the PVC is scheduled.

items.front: Why prefer WaitForFirstConsumer over Immediate?
items.back: Immediate creates the volume before the scheduler picks a node, so it can land in a zone the Pod can't be scheduled into — surfacing later as 'had volume node affinity conflict', which reads as a scheduling bug.

items.front: Does ReadWriteOnce mean one Pod?
items.back: No — one NODE. Several Pods on the same node can mount an RWO volume. ReadWriteOncePod (RWOP) is the one that means exactly one Pod, cluster-wide.

items.front: Reclaim policies, and what Retain leaves behind?
items.back: Delete removes PV and backing storage; Retain leaves the PV in Released with the data intact. It isn't reusable until you clear its claimRef: kubectl patch pv <pv> -p '{"spec":{"claimRef": null}}'

items.front: What must be true before you can grow a PVC?
items.back: allowVolumeExpansion: true on its StorageClass. Patch spec.resources.requests.storage, then check status.capacity — some drivers finish the filesystem resize only after the Pod restarts.

items.front: Which storage detail makes kubectl drain refuse?
items.back: An emptyDir volume — the data would be destroyed, so drain requires --delete-emptydir-data.

items.front: Two default StorageClasses exist. What happens?
items.back: The API accepts it and provisioning becomes non-deterministic. Patch the is-default-class annotation to "false" on the one you don't want.

items.front: Which storage objects have no imperative kubectl generator?
items.back: PersistentVolume, PersistentVolumeClaim and StorageClass — all three must be authored. That is the storage memorisation list.
